title: Bias & Fairness Lab
goal: Your kid finds out that AI has habits it learned from its data: who it pictures by default, which language it answers best, who it leaves out. They guess what AI will do, test it, count the results, compare languages and try to get a fairer answer.
need: A grown-up's account on an AI chat or image tool
A notebook for predictions and tally marks
A second language, if your family has one

academics.subject: Social studies
academics.text: who gets shown, and who gets left out

academics.subject: Digital literacy
academics.text: why AI learns habits from its data

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is telling them AI is unfair and leaving it there. Your job is to run the tests with them, count honestly, and turn what they find into better questions, not into fear.

plan.what: Compare languages and try to fix it (Steps 4 and 5).
Notice AI's defaults when you use it.

troubleshoot.a: That's a real result too. Try a few more jobs or descriptions; patterns often show up only when you count several.
Talk about it. It's the data the AI learned from, not a truth about people. Then try the fix step together.

troubleshoot.q: The tool adds variety on its own
troubleshoot.a: Some tools now mix up who they show on purpose. That's a result too: talk about why the company might do that, then try a description it hasn't fixed yet.

lesson.text: AI learns from huge amounts of writing and pictures made by people, so it picks up their habits: who usually gets shown as a scientist, which language gets the best answers, what's 'normal'. Those habits are called bias. Spotting them is how you get fairer answers.

model.line: The same question in French and in English.
'A family having dinner' came back as the same kind of family, three times.
AI has habits. You have to check, and ask again.

lesson.modelNote: The AI wasn't being mean. It was falling back on its habits, and working best in the language it had seen the most. Noticing that is the first step to getting a fairer answer.

steps.title: Predict the picture
steps.why: A guess written down first makes it a real test, and shows what they already expect.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a few descriptions from the Test ideas card in the Fairness Toolkit at the end of the guide, like 'a scientist' or 'a nurse', and guesses what the AI will show or say.
steps.you: Make your own guesses too, and write both down. Don't explain bias yet; let the test do it.
ask: What do you think it will show for 'a scientist'?
steps.tip: Job titles, family words and 'a kid from...' are the descriptions where habits show up most.

levels.explore: Guess what one picture will look like, and draw it.
levels.develop: Write guesses for four descriptions before testing.
levels.extend: Guess, and also predict which descriptions will show the strongest habit.

steps.title: Test it
steps.why: One try can be luck. A few tries show what the AI does by habit.
steps.kid: Your kid asks the AI for each description, the same way each time, using the Run a fair test card. With an image tool, ask it to draw one. With a chat tool, ask 'Write two sentences about a scientist, and give them a name', then look at the names and he or she.
steps.you: Keep the words exactly the same between tries.
ask: What did it do without being asked?
steps.tip: Leave out details on purpose. What the AI fills in by itself is its habit.

levels.explore: Ask for one description, with a parent, and compare with your drawing.
levels.develop: Test four descriptions, three times each.
levels.extend: Ask the AI why it picked what it did. It can't really see its own reasons, so decide if its answer sounds like a real reason or a good guess.

steps.title: Count what you see
steps.why: Counting turns a feeling into evidence.
steps.kid: Your kid tallies what showed up, using the Count it card: who, how they looked, where, and what was missing.
steps.you: Keep the counting honest, and kind. You're describing the AI's pattern, not judging people.
ask: Who never showed up at all?
steps.tip: 'Who's missing?' is often the most important question in the whole test.

levels.explore: Count one thing, like how many were men and how many were women.
levels.develop: Tally four things for each description, and circle the biggest pattern.
levels.extend: Turn your tallies into a simple chart, and explain what it shows.

steps.title: Compare languages
steps.why: AI usually learned the most from English, so it often works best in English.
steps.kid: Your kid asks the same question in two languages, using the Two languages card, and compares how good, how long and how accurate each answer is.
steps.you: If your family speaks another language, use it. If not, ask the question in a language you don't speak, ask the AI to translate its answer back, and compare it with the answer in yours.
steps.tip: Kids who speak two languages spot this fast, and it makes bias real for them.

levels.explore: Ask a simple question in two languages with a parent, and pick the better answer.
levels.develop: Compare three questions in two languages, and note the differences.
levels.extend: Test a question about your own culture in two languages, and see which knows more.

steps.title: Try to make it fairer
steps.why: Spotting bias matters most when you can do something about it.
steps.kid: Your kid rewrites their prompts to get fairer results, using the Make it fairer card, then tests again and compares.
steps.you: Talk about why it helped. Being specific is how you stay in charge of the AI's habits.
ask: What changed when you were more specific?
What would you tell the people who make the AI?
steps.tip: Describing exactly what you want, instead of trusting the default, is the most useful fix.

levels.explore: Add one detail to your prompt, and see if the picture changes.
levels.develop: Rewrite two prompts to be fairer, test them and compare.
levels.extend: Write a short note to the company that makes the AI, with your evidence.

conclusion.headline: They know AI has habits, and how to work around them.
conclusion.text: Over the next few weeks, look at what they add to a prompt before they hit enter. Typing 'show different kinds of scientists' without being told means they now check the default.
conclusion.celebrate: When they spot a habit and fix their prompt, say: 'You noticed what the AI assumed, and you changed it.'
extensions: Look for the same habits in ads, picture books or video thumbnails
Test a voice assistant: does it understand every family member's voice and accent equally well?
Search your own photo library for 'dog' or 'beach', and see what the photo app finds and what it misses
Find out how one AI company says it tests its tools for fairness

signs: They notice what AI fills in by default
They add detail to prompts to get fairer results
They say why an answer might be different in another language
makeItReal: This week, when you use AI for a picture or an answer together, leave one detail out on purpose, see what it fills in, and talk about why.

fromHome.text: When my kids made a book with AI pictures, the AI didn't always picture the characters the way they described them. And when we use AI in French, the answers are worse than in English.
